malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate memory growth may occur in applications with large caches or persistent data structures, but not from simple, repeated instantiations of a lightweight debugging utility.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, on page load or script execution, the code injects external scripts into the page, including a deprecated version of Ionicons and a remote script (slim.js) hosted on jsDelivr, which itself contains the trojanized jQuery. This enables further malicious code execution and persistence by loading additional payloads from attacker-controlled sources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script injects remote code from attacker-controlled sources without user consent, using a misleading deprecation warning to disguise its activity and facilitate further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject remote scripts or downgrade libraries without explicit user action or clear documentation. Core libraries should not dynamically load external code from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script injection is used in some legitimate plugin loaders, but not in core libraries or without user awareness and explicit opt-in.
key_indicators: Injection of remote scripts from suspicious or attacker-controlled domains
Phony deprecation warnings in console output to mislead users
Use of outdated or deprecated library versions
Chaining to further malicious payloads via dynamic script loading

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, on page load or script execution

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a trojanized version of jQuery in which the 'end' prototype function is maliciously modified to exfiltrate all form data from the page to attacker-controlled domains whenever it is called, either directly or indirectly (e.g., via fadeTo). The package is distributed under many names and versions, often with additional suspicious files and unique exfiltration URLs, indicating a persistent, manually assembled supply chain attack targeting web applications.

attack_chain.action: User installs a malicious npm package containing a trojanized jQuery file (or similar).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present in the project and loaded in the browser.

attack_chain.action: Trojanized jQuery is loaded and used in the web application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious prototype function (end) is available in the global jQuery object.

attack_chain.action: User or application code calls fadeTo or end (directly or indirectly), triggering the malicious end function.
attack_chain.leads_to: Form data is serialized and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled domains.

attack_chain.action: Injected scripts (from icons.js/min.js) load additional remote payloads (e.g., slim.js) from jsDelivr, which may contain further trojanized code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and further compromise of the web application.

behavioral_signatures: Modification of jQuery prototype functions (especially end) to perform network requests

Dynamic injection of remote scripts from non-standard or outdated sources
Presence of phony deprecation warnings in console output

network_indicators: Requests to domains such as *.truex.biz.id, *.hanznesia.my.id, *.api-system.engineer, *.jsdelivr.net/gh/indexsc/libs/slim.js, and other listed campaign domains
AJAX GET requests with hex-encoded form data in query parameters

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code performs a deep merge using jQuery.extend(true, ...) with user-controlled input containing a __proto__ property, resulting in the devMode property being set on Object.prototype and making it globally accessible.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows user input to modify the Object prototype, which can introduce attacker-controlled properties globally and compromise application logic or security boundaries.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, deep merging should only affect the target object, not the global prototype chain. Here, untrusted input is able to pollute the prototype, impacting all objects.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deep merging of configuration objects is common, but should never allow modification of the prototype chain.
key_indicators: Use of __proto__ property in user input
Recursive merge without filtering prototype keys
Global side effects such as {}.devMode === true

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of jQuery allow prototype pollution via the extend() API. Attackers can inject properties into the Object prototype by supplying objects with __proto__, constructor, or prototype keys as input to deep merge operations. This enables privilege escalation, denial of service, or arbitrary code path manipulation in applications that use jQuery.extend(true, ...) with untrusted input, as malicious properties become globally accessible on all objects.

attack_chain.leads_to: Application processes the input using unsafe deep merge or mapping.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code performs a deep merge using jQuery.extend(true, ...) with user-controlled input containing a __proto__ property, resulting in the devMode property being set on Object.prototype and making it globally accessible.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows user input to modify the Object prototype, which can introduce attacker-controlled properties globally and compromise application logic or security boundaries.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, deep merging should only affect the target object, not the global prototype chain. Here, untrusted input is able to pollute the prototype, impacting all objects.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deep merging of configuration objects is common, but should never allow modification of the prototype chain.
key_indicators: Use of __proto__ property in user input
Recursive merge without filtering prototype keys
Global side effects such as {}.devMode === true

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of jQuery allow prototype pollution via the extend() API. Attackers can inject properties into the Object prototype by supplying objects with __proto__, constructor, or prototype keys as input to deep merge operations. This enables privilege escalation, denial of service, or arbitrary code path manipulation in applications that use jQuery.extend(true, ...) with untrusted input, as malicious properties become globally accessible on all objects.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits user-controlled JSON or object containing a __proto__ property.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application processes the input using unsafe deep merge or mapping.

attack_chain.leads_to: The Object prototype is polluted with attacker-controlled properties.

slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time (module-level code), the code defines and initializes Ember.js application modules and components, reading configuration data from a meta tag named "dummy/config/environment" in the HTML document, resulting in setting up the application environment without external network communication.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The provided code is a typical Ember.js application setup defining modules, components, initializers, and templates. It reads configuration from a meta tag in the HTML document and initializes the application accordingly. There is no evidence of obfuscation, data exfiltration, destructive DOM manipulation, or any suspicious conditional logic. The code structure and behavior align with standard Ember.js application boilerplate and usage patterns. Compared to the known malicious patterns, this code does not export null or empty modules, does not perform destructive DOM operations, nor does it contain trivial or spam-like code. Therefore, it is very likely benign.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code defines the module as an ES module and exports a null default value, resulting in no data processing or side effects.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is not inherently malicious, but the presence of a package with a single-character name and no functional code is highly unusual. Such packages are often created unintentionally due to typographical errors and can be abused in the future if the code is updated to include malicious payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages typically provide useful functionality or utilities, whereas this package exports only a null value and performs no operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Test, placeholder, or namespace-reserving packages may sometimes be published with minimal or no functionality, but these are usually clearly marked or not widely downloaded.
key_indicators: Single-character package name ('-')
index.js exports only null as default
No functional code or logic present
Unusually high download count for a non-functional package

package_info.why_malicious: The package '-' is not currently malicious, but its existence and high download count are due to accidental installations caused by typographical errors in npm commands. Its presence in projects is unintentional and could be abused in the future if the package contents change to include malicious code. The risk is that such packages can be silently included in builds, creating a potential supply chain attack vector by providing an opportunity for attackers to later introduce malicious payloads into a widely distributed, trusted dependency.

attack_chain.action: Accidental installation of the '-' package due to typographical errors in npm commands or package.json dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package is included in the project, potentially as a placeholder for future malicious code, creating a supply chain risk if the package contents are updated with malicious payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of single-character or command-like package names in dependencies (e.g., '-', 'i', 'g', 'D')
Packages with no functional code or only skeleton code (e.g., exporting null or empty modules)
High download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation
file_indicators: package.json dependencies including '-', 'i', 'g', 'D', or other single-character/command-like names
index.js file that only exports null or an empty module
package.json scripts section with non-functional or placeholder scripts referencing missing files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan package.json and package-lock.json for dependencies with suspicious names such as '-', 'i', 'g', or names matching npm command flags. Flag packages that have no functional code or only export null/empty modules in their main files. Check for non-functional npm scripts referencing missing files. Monitor for sudden inclusion of such packages in projects, especially if not explicitly added by developers, and alert on high download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (when the web application loads in the browser), the code checks for the presence and value of the VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY environment variable and verifies if the application is running on a hardcoded list of allowed domains in production; if these checks fail, it sets document.body.innerHTML to an empty string, resulting in the entire web page being erased and the application rendered unusable for end users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.
key_indicators: Destructive DOM manipulation (document.body.innerHTML = '')
Hardcoded allow-list of domains in frontend code
Conditional logic tied to environment variables (VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY, NODE_ENV)
Sabotage logic triggered only in production environments
Absence of user notification or error handling before destructive action

Review for the presence of sabotage logic that disables the application outside of specific domains, especially when tied to environment variables like VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY and NODE_ENV.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of obfuscated JavaScript files during npm install, test, or import. Flag packages that spawn detached Node.js processes or create local HTTP servers on non-standard ports such as 3004. Detect creation of suspicious files including node.compress.exe, node.compress.lock.log, and batch files with random names in temp directories. Watch for outbound HTTP requests to unknown or suspicious domains and for local servers listening for command parameters. Use static analysis to identify high-entropy, obfuscated code and dynamic analysis to observe process spawning, file creation, and network activity indicative of RAT behavior.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code immediately throws an error by invoking a function that always throws, preventing any further execution and breaking all dependent applications.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The main entry point of the package is replaced with code that unconditionally throws an error as soon as the package is imported, which is a clear sign of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A normal package should provide its documented functionality and allow consumers to use its API. Instead, this version ensures that any attempt to use the package results in an immediate and unrecoverable error, violating the trust and expectations of downstream users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A package might throw an error if a critical dependency is missing, if the environment is unsupported, or if the user is using a deprecated API. However, it is not legitimate for a widely used package to throw an error unconditionally for all consumers, as this constitutes a denial of service.
key_indicators: Main entry point (index.js) contains only an error-throwing statement
Complete removal of all functional code from the package
Error is thrown immediately upon import, with no conditional logic
No legitimate functionality or exports are provided

package_info.why_malicious: The faker@6.6.6 package was intentionally sabotaged by its maintainer as a form of protestware. In this version, all original source code was removed and replaced with a single statement that throws an error immediately upon import. This deliberate action causes any project that installs or upgrades to this version to fail at runtime, resulting in a denial-of-service condition for all dependent applications and pipelines. The package is therefore malicious at the macro level due to its intentional disruption of the software supply chain.

attack_chain.action: Maintainer publishes a new major version (6.6.6) of faker with all original source code removed and replaced by code that throws an error immediately upon import.
attack_chain.leads_to: Any project that upgrades to or installs faker@6.6.6 will immediately fail at runtime due to the thrown error.

attack_chain.action: Consumers of the package experience denial of service as their applications, build pipelines, or test suites fail to start or execute.
attack_chain.leads_to: Disruption of development workflows and production systems that rely on faker, potentially causing widespread outages and productivity loss.

behavioral_signatures: Main entry point (index.js) throws an error immediately upon import
All functional code removed in a new major version and replaced with a single error-throwing statement
Sudden, unexplained breaking change in a widely used package that causes all consumers to fail
file_indicators: index.js or main file reduced to a single error-throwing statement
Absence of expected source files or directories in the package (e.g., lib/, src/)
Drastic reduction in package size compared to previous versions
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for major version updates of critical dependencies that remove all or most source code, especially if the main entry point throws an error or disables all functionality. Automated dependency analysis tools should flag packages where the main export is a function that only throws, or where the package contents are drastically reduced compared to previous versions. Review changelogs and diffs for sudden, unexplained code removal and error-throwing logic in the main entry point.
